content: The following studies and articles provide insights into the management, diagnosis, and epidemiology of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and genital ulcer diseases (GUD) across various regions and healthcare settings: 1. A study published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS in 2001 examined the management of sexually transmitted diseases in urban pharmacies in The Gambia. 2. Harrison et al. (1998) explored strategies to improve the quality of STI case management in rural South Africa, as reported in AIDS. 3. Wilkinson et al. (2001) discussed public-private health sector partnerships for STI control in South Africa, based on experiences in Hlabisa, as published in the South African Medical Journal. 4. Iipinge and Pretorius (2012) evaluated the delivery and quality of STI treatment by private general practitioners in Windhoek, Namibia, in the Global Journal of Health Science. 5. Biter et al. (2002) investigated the quality of STI management in six West African countries, as detailed in Sante. 6. Alemayehu and Godana (2015) assessed the knowledge and practices of clinicians regarding syndromic management of STIs in public health facilities in the Gamo Gofa Zone, South Ethiopia, as published in the Journal of Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 7. Ward et al. (2003) highlighted the potential of community pharmacists in providing syndromic treatment for STIs as an underutilized HIV prevention strategy, as reported in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 8. Sharma et al. (2016) evaluated skill-oriented training for enhanced syndromic case management of reproductive tract infections and STIs among healthcare providers in Gujarat, India, as published in the Indian Journal of Community Medicine. 9. Bogaerts et al. (1989) investigated the etiology of genital ulceration in Rwanda, as reported in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 10. Zimba et al. (2011) studied the etiology of STIs in Maputo, Mozambique, as detailed in the Journal of Infection in Developing Countries. 11. Phiri et al. (2013) examined the etiology of genital ulcer disease and its association with HIV infection in Malawi, as published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 12. Orle et al. (1996) developed a simultaneous PCR detection method for Haemophilus ducreyi, Treponema pallidum, and herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 from genital ulcers, as reported in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology. 13. Morse et al. (1997) compared clinical diagnosis with laboratory and molecular methods for diagnosing genital ulcer disease in Lesotho, highlighting its association with HIV infection, as published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 14. Hoyo et al. (2003) proposed syndromic criteria to improve the diagnosis of genital ulcer disease, as reported in the American Journal of Epidemiology. 15. Kamya et al. (1995) reported a high prevalence of genital herpes among patients with genital ulcer disease in Uganda, as published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 16. Harms et al. (1994) described the pattern of STIs in a Malagasy population, as detailed in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 17. O’Farrell et al. (1991) investigated genital ulcer disease in women in Durban, South Africa, as reported in Genitourinary Medicine. 18. Vora et al. (2011) conducted a clinico-epidemiological study of STIs in males at a rural-based tertiary care center in India, as published in the Indian Journal of Sexually Transmitted Diseases and AIDS. 19. O’Farrell et al. (1991) also studied genital ulcer disease in men in Durban, South Africa, as detailed in Genitourinary Medicine. 20. Mertz et al. (1998) investigated the etiology of genital ulcers and the prevalence of HIV coinfection in 10 U.S. cities, as reported by the Genital Ulcer Disease Surveillance Group in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 21. Gomes et al. (2007) examined the clinical, microbiological, and histopathological characteristics of genital ulcers in women, as published in the Brazilian Journal of Infectious Diseases. 22. Lewis et al. (2012) studied the prevalence and associations of genital ulcer and urethral pathogens in men presenting with genital ulcer syndrome in South Africa, as reported in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 23. Becker et al. (2010) investigated the etiology and determinants of STIs in Karnataka, South India, as published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 24. Mertz et al. (1998) conducted a study in Jackson, Mississippi, using a multiplex PCR assay to investigate genital ulcers, revealing a high prevalence of chancroid and HIV infection, as reported in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 25. Bruisten et al. (2001) evaluated diagnostic methods for genital ulcer disease in an STI clinic in Amsterdam, as published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology. Finally, a systematic search on genital ulcer syndromes retrieved 14,190 results, with 30% identified as duplicates. The preand post-deduplication results are summarized in the study.
